Technical Details

Source: vignettes/technical-details.Rmd
technical-details.Rmd

This vignette describes the mathematical framework and computational implementation of the JointODE model, which jointly models longitudinal biomarker trajectories and survival outcomes through a coupled ordinary differential equation (ODE) system.

Model Framework

Longitudinal Sub-Model

The observed biomarker measurements are modeled as:

V_{ij}=m_i(T_{ij})+\varepsilon_{ij},\quad i=1,\ldots,n,\quad j=1,\ldots,n_i

where:

  • V_{ij}: Observed biomarker value for subject i at time T_{ij}
  • m_i(t): True underlying biomarker trajectory
  • \varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{e}^{2}): Measurement error

The evolution of biomarker trajectories is governed by a second-order linear differential equation, which captures the dynamic behavior of the system:

\ddot{m}(t) + 2 \xi \omega \dot{m}(t) + \omega^2 m(t) = k \omega^2 \mu(t),

where \xi denotes the damping ratio, \omega represents the natural frequency, k serves as a scaling parameter, and \mu(t) characterizes the external input function driving the system.

To accommodate subject-specific heterogeneity and incorporate covariate effects, we extend this framework through a linear mixed-effects modeling approach. The second-order differential equation is reformulated as:

\ddot{m}_{i}(t) = \mathbf{Z}_i(t)^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{b}_{i}),

where the model components are defined as follows:

  • \mathbf{Z}_i(t) = [m_i(t), \dot{m}_i(t), \mathbf{X}_i(t)^{\top}]^{\top} constitutes the feature vector, comprising the biomarker level, its first derivative, and covariate information
  • \boldsymbol{\beta} = [\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}, \boldsymbol{\beta}_{X}^{\top}]^{\top} represents the vector of fixed-effect parameters
  • \mathbf{b}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b) denotes the subject-specific random-effect vector, assumed to follow a multivariate normal distribution with zero mean and covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b

Within this hierarchical framework, the subject-specific dynamic parameters are derived as:

  • Natural frequency: \omega_i = \sqrt{-(\beta_{1} + b_{i,1})}
  • Damping ratio: \xi_i = -\frac{\beta_{2} + b_{i,2}}{2\omega_i}
  • Excitation effects: k \mu_i(t) = \frac{(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{X} + \mathbf{b}_{i,X})^{\top} \mathbf{X}_i(t)}{\omega_i^2}

This hierarchical structure allows each subject to have unique dynamics around the population-average trajectory.

Survival Sub-Model

The hazard function incorporates the biomarker dynamics:

\lambda_i(t) = \lambda_{0}(t)\exp\left[\alpha_1 m_i(t) + \alpha_2 \dot{m}_i^{\gamma}(t) + \mathbf{W}_i(t)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}\right]

where:

  • \lambda_{0}(t): Baseline hazard function
  • \mathbf{W}_i(t): Covariate vector (time-dependent or time-independent) with regression coefficients \boldsymbol{\phi}
  • \gamma \in \{0, 1, 2\}: Power parameter for the velocity contribution, where \gamma = 0 corresponds to no velocity effect (i.e., \alpha_2 term is excluded), \gamma = 1 yields linear velocity effect \alpha_2\dot{m}_i(t), and \gamma = 2 yields quadratic velocity effect \alpha_2[\dot{m}_i(t)]^2

ODE System

The complete system couples the biomarker trajectory dynamics with the survival process. The state vector \mathbf{s}_i(t) = (\Lambda_i(t), m_i(t), \dot{m}_i(t))^{\top} evolves according to:

\frac{d\mathbf{s}_i}{dt} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_i(t) \\ \dot{m}_i(t) \\ \mathbf{Z}_i(t)^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{b}_i) \end{pmatrix}

with initial conditions \mathbf{s}_i(0) = (0, m_{i0}, \dot{m}_{i0})^{\top}, where m_{i0} and \dot{m}_{i0} are the initial biomarker value and velocity for subject i.

Model Parameterization

For parameter estimation, we need to specify parametric forms for the model components.

Baseline Hazard Parameterization:

The log baseline hazard is parameterized using B-splines for flexibility:

\log\lambda_0(t) = \boldsymbol{\eta}^{\top} \mathbf{B}^{(\lambda)}(t)

where \mathbf{B}^{(\lambda)}(t) = [B_1^{(\lambda)}(t), \ldots, B_q^{(\lambda)}(t)]^{\top} is a B-spline basis with q basis functions, and \boldsymbol{\eta} \in \mathbb{R}^q are the corresponding coefficients.

Therefore, the complete hazard function is:

\lambda_i(t) = \exp\left[\boldsymbol{\eta}^{\top} \mathbf{B}^{(\lambda)}(t) + \alpha_1 m_i(t) + \alpha_2 \dot{m}_i^{\gamma}(t) + \mathbf{W}_i(t)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}\right]

Trajectory Dynamics Parameterization:

The second-order ODE governing the biomarker trajectory incorporates both fixed and random effects:

\ddot{m}_{i}(t) = (\beta_{1} + b_{i,1}) m_{i}(t) + (\beta_{2} + b_{i,2}) \dot{m}_{i}(t) + (\boldsymbol{\beta}_{X} + \mathbf{b}_{i,X})^{\top} \mathbf{X}_i(t)

This can be compactly written as \ddot{m}_{i}(t) = \mathbf{Z}_i(t)^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{b}_i), where the parameters control the system dynamics through physical interpretations.

Parameter Estimation via the EM Algorithm

The model contains continuous random effects \mathbf{b}_i \in \mathbb{R}^p as latent variables, necessitating the use of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation.

The marginal likelihood for subject i is obtained by integrating over the unobserved random effects:

L_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \int p(\mathbf{V}_i | \mathbf{b}_i) \cdot p(T_i, \delta_i | \mathbf{b}_i) \cdot p(\mathbf{b}_i) \, d\mathbf{b}_i

where \boldsymbol{\theta} = (\boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\eta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \gamma, \sigma_e^2, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b) includes all model parameters, with the following likelihood components:

\begin{aligned} \text{Longitudinal:} \quad & p(\mathbf{V}_i | \mathbf{b}_i) = \prod_{j=1}^{n_i} \mathcal{N}(V_{ij}; m_{i}(T_{ij}|\mathbf{b}_i), \sigma_e^2)\\ \text{Survival:} \quad & p(T_i, \delta_i | \mathbf{b}_i) = [\lambda_{i}(T_i)]^{\delta_i} \exp[-\Lambda_{i}(T_i)]\\ \text{Random Effects:} \quad & p(\mathbf{b}_i) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b) \end{aligned}

where m_{i}(t|\mathbf{b}_i) denotes the trajectory solution with random effects \mathbf{b}_i.

E-Step: Computing Posterior Distributions

For each subject i:

Step 1: Compute the log-posterior density of \mathbf{b}_i

The log-posterior density is given by: \ell_{i}(\mathbf{b}) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma_e^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}[V_{ij} - m_{i}(T_{ij}|\mathbf{b})]^2 + \delta_i\log\lambda_{i}(T_i|\mathbf{b}) - \Lambda_{i}(T_i|\mathbf{b}) - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b^{-1}\mathbf{b}

Note that the hazard function depends on the trajectory m_i(t|\mathbf{b}) which is influenced by the random effects through the ODE dynamics.

Step 2: Posterior mode identification via Laplace approximation

The posterior mode \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i} is obtained by maximizing the log-posterior using L-BFGS-B optimization: \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{b}} \ell_{i}(\mathbf{b})

Subsequently, posterior moments are computed via the Laplace approximation:

  • Posterior mean: \hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i} = \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i} (the mode)
  • Posterior covariance: \hat{\mathbf{V}}_{i} = [-\nabla^2\ell_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i})]^{-1} (inverse Hessian)

where \mathcal{O}_i = \{\mathbf{V}_i, T_i, \delta_i\} denotes the observed data for subject i, and the Hessian \nabla^2\ell_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i}) is computed numerically.

Step 3: Marginal likelihood approximation

The marginal likelihood is approximated using the Laplace method: L_i \approx \exp[\ell_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i})] \cdot (2\pi)^{p/2}|-\nabla^2\ell_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i})|^{-1/2}

where -\nabla^2\ell_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i}) is the observed information matrix (positive definite at the maximum).

M-Step: Parameter Updates

Given the sufficient statistics \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}, \hat{\mathbf{V}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^n from the E-step, the parameter updates are obtained by maximizing the expected complete-data log-likelihood:

\begin{aligned} Q(\boldsymbol{\theta}) &= \sum_{i=1}^n \log p(\mathcal{O}_i, \mathbf{b}_i = \hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i} | \boldsymbol{\theta})\\ &= \underbrace{-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_e^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma_e^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} [V_{ij} - m_{i}(T_{ij}|\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i})]^2}_{\text{Longitudinal component}}\\ &\quad + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n [\delta_i\log\lambda_{i}(T_i) - \Lambda_{i}(T_i)]}_{\text{Survival component}}\\ &\quad + \underbrace{-\frac{n}{2}\log|2\pi\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b| - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \text{tr}[(\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}^{\top} + \hat{\mathbf{V}}_{i})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b^{-1}]}_{\text{Random effects component}} \end{aligned}

Parameter updates:

  • Variance components (closed form):
    • \sigma_e^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} [V_{ij} - m_{i}(T_{ij}|\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i})]^2
    • \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}^{\top} + \hat{\mathbf{V}}_{i})
  • Other parameters (\boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\eta}, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \gamma, \boldsymbol{\phi}): Numerical optimization using gradients derived from Q_{long} + Q_{surv}

Computational Implementation

The M-step requires maximizing Q(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = Q_{long}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + Q_{surv}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) through gradient-based optimization. The following sections derive the necessary gradients for each parameter group.

1. Fixed effects parameters (\boldsymbol{\beta}):

\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} Q = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} \frac{r_{ij}}{\sigma_e^2} \frac{\partial m_{i}(T_{ij}|\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} + \delta_i \frac{\partial \log\lambda_i(T_i)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} - \int_0^{T_i} \lambda_{i}(t) \frac{\partial \log\lambda_i(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} dt\right]

where r_{ij} = V_{ij} - m_i(T_{ij}|\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i) is the residual.

2. Hazard baseline (\boldsymbol{\eta}):

\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\eta}} Q = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\delta_i \mathbf{B}^{(\lambda)}(T_i) - \int_0^{T_i} \lambda_{i}(t) \mathbf{B}^{(\lambda)}(t) dt\right]

3. Association parameters (\alpha_1, \alpha_2):

For \alpha_1: \nabla_{\alpha_1} Q = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\delta_i m_{i}(T_i) - \int_0^{T_i} \lambda_{i}(t) m_{i}(t) dt\right]

For \alpha_2: \nabla_{\alpha_2} Q = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\delta_i \dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}(T_i) - \int_0^{T_i} \lambda_{i}(t) \dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}(t) dt\right]

4. Survival covariates (\boldsymbol{\phi}):

\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} Q = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\delta_i - \Lambda_{i}(T_i)\right] \mathbf{W}_i(T_i)

Computing the Required Sensitivities

The gradient expressions above involve two types of sensitivities that must be computed numerically:

Cumulative Hazard Sensitivities

The cumulative hazard function \Lambda_{i}(T_i) depends on parameters through the instantaneous hazard. For parameters affecting the hazard directly, the sensitivities are computed as:

\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\Lambda_{i}(T_i)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\eta}} &= \int_{0}^{T_i}\lambda_{i}(t)\mathbf{B}^{(\lambda)}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\ \frac{\partial\Lambda_{i}(T_i)}{\partial\alpha_1} &= \int_{0}^{T_i}\lambda_{i}(t)m_{i}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\ \frac{\partial\Lambda_{i}(T_i)}{\partial\alpha_2} &= \int_{0}^{T_i}\lambda_{i}(t)\dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\ \frac{\partial\Lambda_{i}(T_i)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\phi}} &= \int_{0}^{T_i}\lambda_{i}(t)\mathbf{W}_i(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \end{aligned}

For parameters affecting the trajectory m_{i}(t) through the ODE dynamics, the chain rule yields:

\frac{\partial\Lambda_{i}(T_i)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\int_{0}^{T_i}\lambda_{i}(t)\left[\alpha_1\frac{\partial m_{i}(t)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}} + \alpha_2 \frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}(t)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right]\,\mathrm{d}t

where the velocity term derivative depends on \gamma:

\frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}(t)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \begin{cases} 0, & \gamma = 0 \text{ (no velocity effect)} \\ \frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}(t)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}, & \gamma = 1 \text{ (linear velocity)} \\ 2\dot{m}_{i}(t)\frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}(t)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}, & \gamma = 2 \text{ (quadratic velocity)} \end{cases}

Trajectory Sensitivities

The trajectory sensitivities with respect to parameters affecting the ODE system are computed through the chain rule. Since \ddot{m}_{i}(t) = (\boldsymbol{\beta} + \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)^{\top} \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t), we have:

\frac{\partial \ddot{m}_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t) + (\boldsymbol{\beta} + \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)^{\top} \frac{\partial \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}}

where \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t) = [m_{i}(t), \dot{m}_{i}(t), \mathbf{X}_i(t)^{\top}]^{\top}.

The trajectory sensitivities evolve as:

\frac{\partial m_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} = \int_{0}^{t} \frac{\partial\dot{m}_{i}(s)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \,\mathrm{d}s,\quad \frac{\partial\dot{m}_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} = \int_{0}^{t} \frac{\partial \ddot{m}_{i}(s)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \,\mathrm{d}s

Numerical Methods

Two approaches for computing sensitivities:

Forward Sensitivity Method

Augment the ODE system with sensitivity equations with respect to \boldsymbol{\beta}:

\frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix} \Lambda_{i}(t) \\ m_{i} \\ \dot{m}_{i} \\ \frac{\partial \Lambda_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\eta}} \\ \frac{\partial \Lambda_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\alpha}} \\ \frac{\partial m_{i}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \\ \frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \\ \frac{\partial \Lambda_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_{i}(t) \\ \dot{m}_{i}(t) \\ (\boldsymbol{\beta} + \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)^{\top} \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t) \\ \lambda_{i}(t)\mathbf{B}^{(\lambda)}(t) \\ \lambda_{i}(t)\begin{bmatrix}m_{i}(t) \\ \dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}(t)\end{bmatrix} \\ \frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \\ \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t) + (\boldsymbol{\beta} + \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)^{\top} \frac{\partial \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \\ \lambda_{i}(t) \left[\alpha_1\frac{\partial m_{i}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} + \alpha_2 \frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}}\right] \end{bmatrix}

where \mathbf{Z}_{i}(t) = [m_{i}(t), \dot{m}_{i}(t), \mathbf{X}_i(t)^{\top}]^{\top}, and the last component uses the piecewise derivative for \frac{\partial \dot{m}_{i}^{\gamma}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} as defined above.

Inference

Subject-Specific Dynamics

For each subject i, the dynamics are characterized by: \omega_i = \sqrt{-(\beta_{1} + b_{i,1})}, \quad \xi_i = -\frac{\beta_{2} + b_{i,2}}{2\omega_i}

These yield interpretable quantities:

  • Natural period: T_i = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_i}
  • Damping ratio: \xi_i determines oscillatory behavior
    • \xi_i < 1: Underdamped (oscillatory)
    • \xi_i = 1: Critically damped
    • \xi_i > 1: Overdamped (non-oscillatory)

Population-Level Parameters

The fixed effects (\beta_1, \beta_2) represent the population-average dynamics: - Population natural frequency: \omega_0 = \sqrt{-\beta_{1}} - Population damping ratio: \xi_0 = -\frac{\beta_{2}}{2\omega_0}

The random effects variance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b quantifies between-subject heterogeneity in dynamics.

Delta Method for Derived Parameters

We use the delta method to obtain standard errors for \omega_0 and \xi_0:

\frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial \beta_{1}} = -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{-\beta_{1}}}, \quad \frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial \beta_{2}} = 0

\frac{\partial \xi_0}{\partial \beta_{1}} = -\frac{\beta_{2}}{4(-\beta_{1})^{3/2}}, \quad \frac{\partial \xi_0}{\partial \beta_{2}} = -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{-\beta_{1}}}

The variance-covariance matrix for (\omega_0, \xi_0) is: \text{Var}\begin{pmatrix}\omega_0 \\ \xi_0\end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{J} \text{Var}\begin{pmatrix}\beta_{1} \\ \beta_{2}\end{pmatrix} \mathbf{J}^{\top}

where the Jacobian matrix is: \mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial \beta_{1}} & \frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial \beta_{2}} \\ \frac{\partial \xi_0}{\partial \beta_{1}} & \frac{\partial \xi_0}{\partial \beta_{2}} \end{pmatrix}

Standard Errors

Standard errors for model parameters can be obtained using Louis’ Method:

Compute the observed information matrix accounting for the missing data structure: \mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{\partial^2 \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}^2} = \mathcal{I}_c(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - \mathcal{I}_m(\boldsymbol{\theta}) where \mathcal{I}_c is the complete-data information and \mathcal{I}_m is the missing information due to unobserved random effects.
